html_en:
The AI industry is accelerating toward a moment of profound structural change — in how software gets built, how knowledge gets shared, and perhaps how human expertise gets valued. Today's conversation spans all three.

🏗️ The Infrastructure Reckoning

Shawn Wang (@swyx) dropped what may be the most understated observation of the week: "we are going to have to Rebuild So. Much. Infra. for the age of Software Factories." It's a short tweet that gestures at something enormous. The tooling, the pipelines, the observability layers — most of it was designed for humans writing code, not agents generating it at scale.

This theme found a more concrete expression in Aaron Levie's thoughtful breakdown of what Claude's integration with Slack actually represents. It's not a chatbot you talk to, he argues — it's a coworker that operates in shared spaces, which creates an entirely different set of permissions and access questions:

"The agent needs to instead be like any other user in the system, and you need to be thoughtful about what it should have access to, and make sure its information that is safe to share with that group."
— @levie

The implication is substantial: every enterprise deploying agents will need to redesign their access control and data architecture from first principles. Meanwhile, on the tooling front, Guillermo Rauch (@rauchg) flagged that a significantly faster GLM is now live on Vercel, and shared that the token recovery data from Vercel AI Gateway is "truly astonishing."

🧠 Are We Building a School for AGI?

The most intellectually rich content today came from Dan Shipper's interview with Edwin Chen, CEO of Surge AI — a company that's quietly crossed $1 billion in revenue training frontier models, without raising outside capital. Watch/Listen: Building a School Where AI Models Learn About Humanity — AI & I by Every.

Chen's framing of his work is striking:

"We are building this school for AGI, the school where AI models come to learn about humanity, where we teach them how to run the world. It's almost like the models are children, where they arrive unformed, and then they leave smarter and more creative and more thoughtful and ready to operate in the messiness of the world."
— Edwin Chen, AI & I

The conversation traces how rapidly the benchmarks themselves have had to evolve — from middle-school math (GSM8K, where early GPT models scored around 20%) to research-level mathematics. Chen describes OpenAI's recent result disproving an Erdős conjecture using novel algebraic geometry techniques, and shares a telling anecdote: Fields Medalist Timothy Gowers initially misread the result, and upon realizing AI had found a counterexample rather than an upper bound, was relieved — because it meant mathematicians might still have a unique role to play for "another year, maybe a couple of years."

"You have one of the world's greatest mathematicians being relieved that AI isn't as far as he thought, because it actually means that at least for maybe another year, maybe a couple of years, he and other mathematicians will still have this unique role to play in pushing mathematics forward."
— Edwin Chen

Shipper pushes back throughout — arguing that LLMs have no intrinsic motivation, no drive to explore — while Chen, a believer in scaling laws, sees something closer to general capability emerging. The conversation also surfaces a sharp critique of engagement-optimized models: Chen describes spending 20 rounds polishing a pointless email with one model before Claude finally told him to just send it. His "Hemingway Bench" found models inserting a metaphor into every single sentence — a textbook case of hacking the metric rather than improving the writing.

🎤 How to Give a Talk That Actually Lands

With AI Engineering World's Fair next week, @swyx published a genuinely excellent thread on giving technical talks — drawing on thousands of hours of engineer- and researcher-focused presentations. The whole thread is worth saving, but a few highlights stand out:

"Have a Thesis Slide. You've been in that talk where everyone gets their phone out to take a photo of the slide. You are much more likely to have a viral talk/slide if you have a single viral slide. You are much more likely to have a viral slide if you TRY and most people do not TRY. Your slides have a power law — don't spend 5% of your time each on 20 slides, spend 80% of your time on 1 slide and have the rest build up to that 1 slide."
— @swyx
"How to shill your product/company without feeling salesy: teach me everything I didn't know I should know about the problems you solve, and then you shall have earned the right to convince me you are the guys to trust to solve it once and for all."
— @swyx

The counsel on data-driven talks is particularly sharp: "Present pretty charts and surprising, authoritative numbers. Done well, it will feel like my obvious conclusion from objectively looking at the data you presented, not you feeding the conclusion to me." That's not just advice about slides — it's a philosophy of persuasion.

⚡ Quick Signals

  • Claude Design impresses: @petergyang tested Claude Design on a mobile app repo and found it reproduced screens faithfully — though the model started asking to conserve tokens after just one prompt. Thrift, apparently, is now a personality trait.
  • Google's Project Genie wins big: @GoogleLabs announced Project Genie won the Cannes Lions Grand Prix for AI Craft — a reminder that creative industry recognition for AI work is now firmly mainstream.
  • Cursor ↔ Notion: @ryolu_ dropped a demo showing bidirectional integration between Cursor and Notion — use each inside the other. The blurring of "document" and "code environment" continues apace.
  • Entrepreneurship surge incoming: @rauchg made the macro case simply: "AI will bring forth an unprecedented surge in entrepreneurship — from solopreneurs, to the revitalization of the small & medium business segment, to the emergence of the largest companies of our times."
  • Databricks deep dive: @swyx teased a wide-ranging podcast from Data + AI Summit covering why Databricks beat Snowflake, the fate of MosaicML and DBRX, and whether databases, operating systems, or networking matter most in the race to the agent cloud.
html_zh:
当AI正在重塑软件开发的底层基础设施，演讲的艺术、智能体协作的边界以及人类独特价值的追问，共同构成了今天这个行业最深层的焦虑与兴奋。

🎤 如何做一场真正有价值的技术演讲

AI工程师周（AI Engineer World's Fair）下周即将开幕，swyx 在参加完演讲者备会后，分享了一份言辞犀利的演讲指南。这不是泛泛的PPT技巧，而是从观摩数千场工程师与研究员演讲中提炼出的真知灼见。

"要有论点幻灯片。你一定参加过那种演讲——台下所有人突然掏出手机拍照。因为人们看到图片的频率是看视频的1000倍，你更有可能凭一张爆款幻灯片让整场演讲被广泛传播。大多数人根本没有刻意尝试做到这一点。"
—— @swyx

他的建议直白到有点不客气：AI生成图片请控制在最多4张；把代码放上屏幕（"工程师喜欢鸡蛋里挑骨头"）；音频差的演讲是死局；以及那句最被忽视的忠告——

"每场演讲只有一张'如果你只记住一件事'的卡片。太多人根本没用上它，更多人压根没规划它。你只有一次机会，好好用。"
—— @swyx

值得一提的是他关于"如何卖货不让人反感"的洞见：先把你所解决问题的一切来龙去脉教给听众，然后你才赢得了让他们相信你的资格。这条规则适用于演讲，也适用于整个行业的内容营销。

🤖 智能体协作：Claude进驻Slack，意味着什么？

Box 的 CEO Aaron Levie 对 Anthropic 将 Claude 以"同事"身份集成进 Slack 的发布，写下了迄今最清晰的产品层面解读。他点出了一个大多数人忽略的关键细节：这不是你的私人AI助手，而是一个拥有独立权限体系的共享智能体。

"这个智能体同事需要拥有自己的资源、工具和数据访问权限。这和你把自己的资源授权给它完全不同——因为那样的话，它可能会把你的私人资源意外分享给任何人。这个智能体应该像系统里的任何其他用户一样存在，你需要认真思考它应该访问什么，确保那些信息对整个群组是安全可共享的。"
—— @levie

Levie 进一步描绘了这一模式的实际应用：连接 Box 后，Claude 可以访问销售材料、品牌指南、产品路线图文档，乃至法律合同——所有这些对应团队成员都有访问权限的内容。与此同时，@ryolu_ 展示了另一个集成方向：在 Notion 里用 Cursor，在 Cursor 里用 Notion，两大生产力工具的边界正在悄然消融。

🏗️ 软件工厂时代：我们需要重建多少基础设施？

swyx 今天发出了一条字数不多但分量极重的推文：

"我们将不得不为软件工厂时代重建极其大量的基础设施。"
—— @swyx

这与 Guillermo Rauch（Vercel CEO）的观察形成呼应。他指出 Vercel AI Gateway 恢复的 token 数量和运行时间数据令人震惊，并同步上线了更快的 GLM 模型。在他看来，这一切终将汇聚成一股创业浪潮：

"AI 将带来前所未有的创业热潮——从独立创业者，到中小企业的复兴，再到我们这个时代最大公司的崛起……而它将为所有这一切提供地基。"
—— @rauchg

同一天，swyx 还在 Databricks Data+AI Summit 上做了一期深度播客访谈，话题横跨 Databricks 如何击败 Snowflake、MosaicML 的命运、以及在一家估值 1750 亿美元的巨头内部如何维系研究型初创文化。Watch/Listen: swyx × Databricks 高管深度对谈。

🧠 当AI能证明数学猜想，人类还剩什么？

Watch/Listen: Building a School Where AI Models Learn About Humanity — AI & I by Every

这是今天最值得深思的内容。Dan Shipper 采访了 Surge AI 的 CEO Edwin Chen。Surge 是为 OpenAI、Anthropic 等前沿实验室提供专家数据的机构，收入突破10亿美元，却从未对外融资。

Edwin 将 Surge 的工作比作为 AGI 建造的一所学校——

"AI 模型来这里学习关于人类的一切，我们教它们如何运转这个世界。就像孩子们一样，它们未经雕琢地到来，然后离开时变得更聪明、更有创造力、更善于思考，准备好在混乱的现实世界中运作。"
—— Edwin Chen，AI & I 播客

对话中最令人印象深刻的，是关于 AI 证伪 Erdős 猜想这一事件的讨论。Edwin 分享了菲尔兹奖得主 Timothy Gowers 的反应——他最初以为模型证明了上界，吓得不轻；第二天发现只是反例，顿时松了口气：

"他感到庆幸，因为这意味着至少在未来一两年里，他和其他数学家还有独特的位置，还能继续推动数学前进。你想想，世界上最伟大的数学家之一，居然是这样看待 AI 的。"
—— Edwin Chen，AI & I 播客

而 Dan Shipper 则坚持认为，即便 AI 能力指数级增长，"设定目标"这件事依然是人类的专属领域——LLM 没有内在驱动力，没有自发探索的欲望，也无法凭空改变自己的心意。这场对话没有给出确定答案，但它精准地触碰到了当下整个行业最深的焦虑：我们究竟在为什么而努力？
